devpost_page.title: Campfire
devpost_page.tagline: Campfire is an AI that turns your group's trip chat into a shared story.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The best parts of trips rarely make it into photo albums. All of the information ends up living in the group chat, like the voice note that everyone replayed, the joke that lasted five days for no reason, and the friend that took all of the photos but barely appeared in any. Not even a month later, most of these moments are usually buried under hundreds of messages, never to be seen again. We built Campfire to bring all of this information to light, both during the duration of the trip and afterwards.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Campfire joins the WhatsApp group chat your group is using, and after someone types /campfire start , everyone keeps talking in the group like usual. Campfire captures the trip’s messages, photos, voice memos, and locations mentioned. Each night at a set time, it sends a narrated recap back to the chat, detailing everything that happened that day. Then, when the trip ends (when someone uses the command /campfire end ), the group can open Around the Campfire , a story player that moves through the trip’s locations while narration, captions, and real voice memos by members of the group bring the moments back to life. Also, we made sure to make privacy a big part of the experience. Campfire announces when a trip starts and stops capturing no matter what when hit with /campfire end . It also supports the command /campfire off the record and /campfire on the record , which stop tracking the conversation and restart tracking the conversation respectively. Finally, Campfire also lets group members remove a captured message with /campfire forget . It does not read ordinary direct messages between people, and the flexibility in stopping the tracking and deletion of messages makes sure users feel comfortable with having it in the conversation. The app also shows how a finished story can lead into the next possible trip, as trip suggestions are informed by what the group said they enjoyed or found difficult, just so that the end of one trip can become the start of planning the next one

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: A Node.js service using Baileys connects to the WhatsApp group chat and passes the events as they happen through Redis streams. A Flask backend then stores the trips and messages that come through over and over in PostgreSQL and uses Celery for future story work, which is done in the background. OpenAI then turns the conversation into story segments that are ordered properly, and ElevenLabs handles the voice-note transcription and narration for the whole project. Finally, Backboard provides long term memory to provide to the OpenAI agent which can be used to provide context for memories across different days of the group’s trips, and Muse Spark can add local food and activity suggestions after the nightly recap. We built the frontend playback experience in React and Vite. Its illustrated map follows the story’s stored locations as mentioned in the group messages, and the online player holds the map, the captions from the group chat, and the available audio. Docker Compose runs the local stack, and we set it up to run on a Vultr VPS so that the Campfire bot can keep listening in the chat around the clock. Campfire is available at campfireai.tech.

sections.heading: Challenges and what we learned
sections.text: We learned that a group chat is super messy; people use nicknames, refer to places that aren't explicitly named, reply hours later than they should, and turn one simple sentence into a running joke for no explainable reason. Building Campfire is meant to treat those messages as a shared conversation rather than a folder of files that are hard to interpret. We also had to make the capture window explicit so that all the group members knew what was going on. A memory app only feels welcoming and safe if the group knows when the agent is listening and when they can decide what stays out of the story.

sections.heading: What’s next
sections.text: Our current demo includes prepared trip content, the working capture of information, a story pipeline, and a way to keep the group connected afterwards. Moving forwards, we want to improve the photo-to-place matching and geocoding, implement more features like Side Quests that explain to the rest of the group certain activities that specific people did, and send callbacks on certain anniversaries that reunite the group together around a trip a year later.

devpost_page.title: Bump
devpost_page.tagline: Turn the people you pass into people you know

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The people you'd get along with may already be in the room. You just don't know what to say to them yet. The research points to a consistent problem: Loneliness is common. The WHO Commission on Social Connection estimates that roughly 1 in 6 people worldwide experience loneliness, including around 1 in 5 adolescents and young adults. We misjudge strangers. Commuters expected that talking to a stranger would make their ride worse, yet those who did reported a more positive experience than those who kept to themselves. The fear is worse than the conversation. Across seven studies, people's predicted fears about talking to a stranger were generally worse than their actual experience of the conversation. The problem usually isn't a lack of people to meet. People are already nearby, and uncertainty stops the first conversation. Even when they want to talk, they have almost no context for what to say. "We both like music" is trivia. "You shoot film too?" is a conversation. The common ground already exists. Bump helps you find it when it matters.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Bump gives two people who are already near each other just enough common ground to start talking. Make a profile by talking. Give a short spoken or typed intro. Grok asks up to three follow-up questions, read aloud, and drafts a profile card. You edit and approve every line before anyone sees it. Bump. Tap your phones together. Both people confirm it was really each other before anything is exchanged. Find your overlap. Bump shows the specific interests you share, plus complementary ones: related but different interests, or one person's goal lining up with the other's experience. Those grounded matches become conversation starters. After. A private check-in asks which topics actually came up and whether you'd connect again. That answer never leaves your phone. There's no compatibility percentage and no feed to scroll. Bump isn't deciding who you should be friends with. It answers a much smaller question: What could we talk about right now? Then you put the phones down.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: iOS app (Swift, SwiftUI, iOS 17+) MultipeerConnectivity discovers nearby phones over encrypted peer-to-peer sessions, with a versioned, size-bounded wire protocol. Nearby Interaction (UWB) runs one ranging session per peer to supply distance evidence. Core Motion feeds a spike detector that recognises the bump from the accelerometer. A pairing matcher combines those signals. Both people must confirm, and ambiguous bumps are rejected instead of guessed. ActivityKit/WidgetKit show bump status as a Live Activity. Backend Render hosts bump-api (Node.js 20, zero npm dependencies), which keeps the xAI key off the phone. It routes speech-to-text (Grok voice transcription), text-to-speech for reading onboarding questions aloud, profile drafting, follow-up questions, interest tagging, and talking points. Supabase Realtime handles bump rooms: devices join a room over a secure WebSocket and exchange encrypted bump messages. Rooms disappear when the bump ends. Matching and AI Matching runs on the phone first. It separates shared interests from complementary ones and ranks specific interests above broad categories. Only those grounded pairs go to Grok, which phrases them as conversation starters. It never invents the match. When the server is unavailable or turned off, Apple Foundation Models (where supported) and deterministic templates take over, and the app says which one it used.

sections.heading: Why Bump fits ML / AI / Data Visualization
sections.text: The pipeline is: unstructured human expression → structured, user-approved profile → grounded comparison → high-signal overlap → natural conversation starter Voice and text onboarding turn messy self-description into structured data the user approves. The matching layer then separates broad similarity from specific shared interests, complementary interests, and goal-to-experience links, and puts the most specific overlaps first. Generative AI only comes in after a supported connection exists, to phrase it. The AI helps reveal something already true about two people instead of inventing a reason for them to connect.

sections.heading: Why Bump fits Meta: Bringing People Closer Together with AI
sections.text: Who it's for. Students and people at events, classes and hackathons: anyone standing a few feet from someone they'd like to meet but don't know what to say to. How it strengthens connection. Bump doesn't pull people into another feed. The two people are already in the same room, and Bump gives them one specific, true reason to talk, then gets out of the way. The final interaction isn't another tap. It's putting the phones down and talking. Why AI is essential. Without AI, this is a rigid interest form and a keyword match. With AI, a 45-second spoken intro becomes a structured profile, complementary interests and goal-to-experience links become visible, and the overlap is phrased as a natural opener instead of a list. AI turns "you both tagged music" into something worth saying out loud.

sections.heading: Why Bump fits SpaceXAI: Make it Legendary
sections.text: The real-world challenge. Loneliness is a public health issue: the WHO estimates roughly 1 in 6 people worldwide experience it. Bump targets the moment where connection most often fails, the first hello. Built with Cursor and Grok. We built Bump with Cursor, and Grok handles the parts where language is messy and human: Grok Voice onboarding: transcribes a spoken intro, asks follow-up questions out loud, and drafts an editable profile, so nobody fills out a rigid interest form. Talking points: after two people bump, Grok phrases the grounded overlap into conversation starters. Interest tagging: Grok organises free-text interests into something matchable. Why Grok. Bump needs speech-to-text, text-to-speech and reasoning to work together in one short, spoken conversation. Grok is the only stack we found that covers all three in one API, so a spoken intro becomes a profile in one round of calls instead of three separate vendors. Grok Voice keeps onboarding feeling like a conversation rather than a form, and Grok's reliable structured output means profiles and talking points come back in a shape the app can validate before showing them.

devpost_page.tagline: Pulse uses AR on Snap Spectacles to guide users through CPR in real time with visual and auditory feedback, making life-saving action fast and accessible to everyone.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: When someone collapses from cardiac arrest, every second matters. Yet most people freeze because they are unsure how to help. Only 20% of Americans are current with CPR training, and even fewer feel confident enough to act under pressure. We created Pulse to bridge that gap. Instead of relying on memory or scrambling to find a guide, users can receive calm, step-by-step CPR instructions directly in their field of view. With augmented reality through Snap Spectacles, Pulse empowers anyone to take immediate and effective action during an emergency.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Pulse is an AR application for the Snap Spectacles that provides step-by-step CPR guidance in real time. It has two main components: real-time CPR guidance and a map displaying nearby AEDs for quick retrieval. The CPR guidance component uses Snap Spectacles’ AR capabilities to walk users through each critical step of administering CPR. It directs users on where to place their hands, provides a rhythm to follow for compressions, and measures compression, ensuring accurate and effective compressions. Our AED Map locates nearby registered AED units and displays their locations and approximate distances in the AR world. We have also implemented voice recognition into our map, allowing for hands-free viewing and closing during hectic emergencies.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built Pulse using Lens Studio for Snap Spectacles, integrating pose detection using [David fill this out]. Sensor data from Spectacles helped us track hand movement and force. We also used a voiceML module to integrate voice recognition into our AED locator, allowing for hands-free retrieval.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: GPS Coordinate Precision - We wanted to accurately track AED Locations through GPS, but limited precision of our devices made it difficult to pinpoint exactly where the locations are in real life. We eventually got the AED locations in Pauley Pavilion to be precise within the augmented world, but everywhere else may lack precision. We also ran into the challenge of having to work in a completely new environment as before LA Hacks, none of us had worked with Lens Studio or Snapchat Spectacles. sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of

Overall, it was really cool to be able to have worked with Lens Studio and Spectacles and persevere through the challenges. devpost_page.title: HeirLoom
devpost_page.tagline: Introducing HeirLoom, the first family-oriented database and social platform. Through AI-powered integration, we make family connections easier and protect family heirlooms, stories, and documents!

sections.heading: Pitch
sections.text: They say it takes a village to raise a child, but what if the village no longer exists? Introducing HeirLoom, an iOS app that turns fleeting family memories into a living archive, pairing a real-time conversational voice AI oral historian with a tactile corkboard "tree" of pinned Polaroids and connecting red twine

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The people who raise us shape our values and sense of self, but modern life has scattered families across different cities, demanding careers, and generational divides. Group chats that only awaken for birthday emojis offer the illusion of closeness while irreplaceable oral histories quietly disappear. Most people know little about their lineage past their grandparents, and older generations' life lessons often vanish before anyone writes them down. We wanted to move past sterile family-tree forms and impersonal photo dumps to build a warm, welcoming space where family culture actually lives and grows.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: At the heart of HeirLoom is Loomie, an empathetic voice AI companion. Instead of sending questionnaires or cold text prompts, Loomie speaks aloud with the patience and warmth of an attentive grandchild sitting across the kitchen table. It listens closely, latches onto sensory details like the music playing on an old road trip or the smell of a childhood kitchen, and gently guides elders through their memories without interrupting or feeling clinical. As memories are shared, they materialize onto an interactive family corkboard. Styled like a photo scrapbook or corkboard, the brand design moves away from stereotypical tree iconography and opts for a more homey aesthetic. The app automatically surfaces Sparks (cross-generational threads linking shared passions across decades) like a great-grandfather's mechanical tinkering to a granddaughter studying engineering today. A sepia-toned 3D globe charts family activity across continents, while a native iOS share extension lets anyone drop photos and voice memos straight into the family feed from their camera roll or social media (currently exclusive to instagram).

sections.heading: How we built
sections.text: We created HeirLoom natively in Swift and SwiftUI, custom designing (with no AI generated images or stock assets) an analog aesthetic of parchment paper and Polaroid frames in Figma to keep the interface tactile. For voice interactions, we built a bidirectional audio streaming pipeline using AVFoundation and AVAudioEngine. The app captures live microphone audio, downsamples it to 24 kHz PCM, and streams it over WebSockets to xAI’s real-time voice model. We fine-tuned Voice Activity Detection thresholds so storytellers can pause to reflect mid-sentence without being cut off. To keep conversations grounded, we integrated the Backboard state machine to track dialogue history, relationships, and established facts so Loomie never repeats herself or hallucinates. Once a session ends, an asynchronous Python and FastAPI backend powered by Grok 4.3 analyzes the transcripts, identifies relatives, enriches profiles with historical context, and syncs updates to MongoDB Atlas. Our team worked concurrently across Git branches using Cursor, Claude Code, and Antigravity to build the client and backend services in parallel.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: One of our biggest technical challenges was getting low-latency, full-duplex voice streaming running smoothly in Swift. Balancing raw audio buffers, hardware echo cancellation, and WebSocket throughput under tight frames required extensive profiling to prevent clipping and audio drops. On the visual side, real-world family trees were difficult mathematically. Off-the-shelf tree layouts quickly devolved into overlapping cards and tangled string spaghetti. We had to write a custom dynamic layout algorithm from scratch that calculates pushpin coordinates, organic card rotations, and Bezier red-twine curves that stay clear and legible at any zoom level.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud of how human HeirLoom feels in the hand. Loomie’s patient speech pacing, paired with the personally-designed paper textures, pinned Polaroids, and dynamic red strings, bridges the gap between bleeding-edge AI and cozy nostalgia. Best of all, nobody has to fill out a single form—simply having a natural conversation automatically builds, links, and documents a family tree in real time on a physical device.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Integrating the Backboard.io state machine showed us how critical deterministic state tracking is when grounding conversational agents in personal relational data. On the iOS side, we gained hands-on experience with audio engineering and real-time streaming, while refining our multi-agent workflows across the stack.

sections.heading: What's next for HeirLoom
sections.text: Next, we want to integrate Grok Imagine to turn recorded oral histories into illustrated digital picture books that parents can read to younger children at bedtime. We are also exploring a one-click export pipeline to turn the digital corkboard into a physical coffee-table keepsake book, and a spatial gallery experience designed for Apple Vision Pro/Meta XR Glasses.

devpost_page.tagline: Live forecasts of which satellites are falling, what survives re-entry, and where it could land, powered by GPU Monte Carlo physics and SpacetimeDB.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: In March 2024, a piece of a discarded ISS battery pallet survived re-entry and crashed through the roof of a house in Naples, Florida. Thousands of objects are decaying out of orbit right now. Low Earth orbit holds thousands of short-lived satellites; Starlink alone de-orbits satellites almost daily, and rocket stages and old debris come down too. The public answer to "what's coming down, and where?" is usually a single date with a window of hours, and no idea what actually survives. Break-up and survivability analyses stay inside agencies. We wanted to build the tool we wished existed: a live globe that shows which objects are re-entering, which pieces survive, how heavy and how dangerous they are, and where they could land , with honest uncertainty.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: SKYFALL runs that analysis openly and continuously, on live public data: Track every decaying satellite and rocket body from live orbit data (CelesTrak) and space weather (NOAA SWPC). Forecast when and where each one re-enters, as a probability distribution from about 20,000 simulated futures per object. Break it up into its components (bus, solar arrays, tanks, reaction wheels, batteries, engine parts) and fly every piece down through the atmosphere with heating and melting, thousands of times. Show it all live on a 3D globe. Each object is colored by its earliest plausible re-entry, so anything that could come down within a day stands out. A ring marks objects with at least a 10% chance that a piece lands with more than 15 J of energy, the usual threshold for a dangerous fragment. Clicking an object shows: its live altitude, drop rate, and a probabilistic re-entry window , with a ground corridor that widens as uncertainty grows, impact zones (50% and 90%) where surviving debris could fall, computed from thousands of simulated descents, a 3D model of its components , each with its chance of reaching the ground, surviving mass and impact energy. Hover a part and the globe shows only that part's debris tracks and zones. Forecasts update live as new orbit and space-weather data arrive. If our GPU goes down, the system fails over to CPU automatically and keeps forecasting. Every debris number is labeled as a modeled estimate .

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: SpacetimeDB is the entire backend. It isn't just storage; it's the orchestrator. There is no other server, no side database and no message queue. One TypeScript module (about 2,400 lines: 32 tables, 29 reducers, 4 procedures, 6 schedules) does all of this: Ingest: scheduled procedures make outbound HTTP calls from inside the database to poll NOAA SWPC space weather (every 15 min), CelesTrak decaying objects (every 2 h) and SATCAT decay dates (every 6 h). Job queue with leases: forecast and debris jobs run in two lanes per worker (one bulk job, one fast job), with lease expiry, retries and oldest-first ordering. A scheduled sweep reducer requeues expired leases and evicts silent workers every 2 seconds. Failover as a database rule: CPU workers get no jobs while a healthy GPU worker exists, so failover happens with no extra coordinator. Measured: after we killed the GPU worker, the CPU worker finished the next job 7 seconds later. Chaining: publishing a forecast versions and archives it, then automatically queues a debris job when the chance of re-entry within 72 h is at least 20%. Orbits in the database: SGP4 runs inside the module to keep every object's live position current. Self-scoring: when an official decay date arrives, the module scores the last forecast made before it (hours of error, inside the window or not, lead time). Streaming: the web client subscribes to the tables directly, so the globe updates the moment a result lands, with no polling and no API layer. The w

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Re-entry is hard to predict. Atmospheric density can swing a lot with solar activity, and small errors in drag compound over days. Against official re-entry predictions, our early forecasts ran 7 to 11 hours late . We'd rather show that honestly than hide it, and per-object drag calibration was our biggest fix. Ground truth is scarce. Validating against past re-entries means using only the orbital data available before the event. Historical element sets and recovered-debris locations are hard to find, so building fair test cases was a project in itself. Object physical data is incomplete. Mass, shape and materials aren't public for most objects, so we built sourced archetypes, label every number as real, modeled or assumed, and show a confidence rating. Making failover trustworthy. Getting leases, heartbeats and requeues right, so no job is lost or run twice when the GPU drops, took several iterations. Making debris physics fast enough to run continuously. Batching every particle × component × time step into GPU tensors turned a one-off analysis into something we run for every object about to come down. Time. We built a database-driven job system, two GPU physics engines and a live 3D frontend in one weekend.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A complete live pipeline, from public feeds to GPU physics to a 3D globe, with SpacetimeDB as the only stateful component . GPU-to-CPU failover in 7 seconds , coordinated entirely by database rules. Hundreds of billions of physics steps on a desk-side GX10. Forecasts that score themselves against official decay dates. A per-component survivability view of live re-entries, something the public hasn't had before.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: A real-time database can be the whole backend : ingestion, scheduling, job orchestration, failover, archiving and streaming, with no separate queue or worker coordinator. It made failure handling simpler, not harder. How much re-entry prediction depends on the atmosphere, and why showing uncertainty matters more than a single confident answer. How to write physics that runs fast in parallel on a GPU, and how to keep a CPU path that runs the same physics, visibly degraded, when the GPU is gone. How to work with AI agents as teammates: Grok Bot for planning and coordination, and Cursor for writing and reviewing code.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: As a passionate roboticist, I've witnessed firsthand the transformative revolution unfolding in our field. The industry is increasingly generating rich ecocentric datasets for Physical AI development, which traditionally feed into computationally intensive reinforcement learning policies for task execution. However, this conventional approach remains prohibitively expensive and resource-demanding. This challenge inspired us to explore more efficient alternatives that could democratize advanced robotics capabilities while maintaining the sophisticated functionality needed for real-world applications.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our humanoid robot executes complex, multi-step everyday tasks through advanced spatial understanding and reasoning capabilities. When instructed to "clean up the table" or "sort kitchen items," it intelligently distinguishes between trash and valuable objects, properly disposing of waste while organizing items that should be preserved. The robot demonstrates contextual intelligence by selecting appropriate cleaning tools—knowing when a situation calls for a paper towel versus a brush. This practical reasoning enables it to handle varied household scenarios without specific programming for each task variation, making it truly useful for daily living assistance.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We integrated a Nao Humanoid Robot with a custom controller system to enable walking and arm manipulation capabilities essential for embodied AI tasks. The robot processes multimodal inputs through Gemini's API, accepting both voice commands and visual information from its built-in RGB camera and microphone. When users interact with the robot using natural language, our system breaks down complex commands into manageable action sequences. Each subtask is evaluated using Gemini's spatial understanding capabilities to determine the optimal approach. For example, when asked to clean a coffee spill, the robot: Scans the environment to identify suitable cleaning items Ranks potential tools (prioritizing paper towels and cloths over brushes or scrubbers) Decomposes the task into precise motion sequences (walking to the item, reaching, grasping) Executes actions through Gemini's function calling feature, which triggers the appropriate low-level robot movements This architecture creates a seamless bridge between high-level understanding and physical execution without requiring task-specific training.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Working with the Nao Robot presented significant technical obstacles. The platform's age and outdated infrastructure—requiring Python 2.7 and suffering from minimal documentation—created fundamental difficulties throughout development. Our challenges intensified when the robot's firmware became corrupted during implementation, effectively bricking the device and forcing us to develop custom firmware flashing solutions. This unexpected setback required extensive troubleshooting under tight time constraints. The mathematical complexity of translating visual perception into physical action proved particularly demanding. We needed to implement inverse kinematics algorithms to convert pixel coordinates from visual input into precise joint angles for movement. The coordinate transformation process between the camera frame and robot frame introduced another layer of complexity that required careful mathematical modeling to ensure accurate physical responses to visual stimuli.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: In a remarkably short timeframe, we successfully created a complete robot foundation pipeline for embodied AI that bypasses computationally intensive approaches like reinforcement learning or imitation learning. Despite confronting numerous technical obstacles—including outdated Python dependencies and sparse documentation—we remained persistent in developing alternative solutions without compromising our vision. We're particularly proud of our innovative implementation of Gemini for physical embodiment, positioning ourselves at the forefront of the emerging Physical AI and Embodied AI revolution. By harnessing Gemini's capabilities in this cutting-edge application, we've demonstrated how large foundation models can bridge the gap between perception and physical action without traditional computational burdens. This creative approach to robotics represents exactly where the field is heading—toward more flexible, adaptive systems that can understand and interact with the physical world through advanced AI reasoning rather than rigid programming.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Our project provided invaluable hands-on experience with the mathematical foundations of robotics. We gained practical understanding of coordinate transformation systems and their critical importance in translating between different reference frames. The process of camera calibration became second nature to us, along with appreciating how focal length parameters significantly impact spatial transformations. On the practical side, we learned some hard lessons about hardware management—specifically that interrupting firmware updates can have catastrophic consequences. This experience taught us to always have recovery tools prepared, particularly keeping a bootable flash drive on hand for emergency firmware restoration. These technical insights and practical workflows will prove invaluable for future robotics development work.

This cross-platform validation will help us refine our approach and confirm its flexibility beyond our current implementation. Additionally, we aim to broaden the range of everyday tasks our system can handle, systematically testing and improving its performance across various household scenarios. sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Ground stations are the toll booths of space. A satellite passes overhead for a few minutes, an antenna tracks it, the data comes down, and someone sends a bill. AWS Ground Station charges by the minute. KSAT, the world's largest commercial ground-station operator, reported NOK 2.361B (about USD $234M) in 2025 group revenue across about 2.1 million contacts on about 375 antennas . At that volume, every dropped pass, partial downlink, or "the storm ate my data" email turns into a billing dispute. Right now a person settles each one by hand. They pull the pass log, check space weather, check maintenance notices, read the contract's SLA, and decide whether to issue a credit. It's slow and inconsistent: two analysts can rule differently on the same claim. It's also easy to game. If you know the analyst skips the weather check, you'll blame a storm. We modeled Ground Truth on that operating profile and asked Hyphenate's question: can a finance team hire an autonomous system for this corner of the books, with limited access, a clean record, and the sense to ask when it should?

sections.heading: Is it real enough?
sections.text: Realistic data, a messy problem, and proof that it works. The company. A mid-market ground-station operator in the shape of KSAT: hundreds of antennas, millions of contacts a year, minute-based billing, and a flood of customer credit claims when a pass fails. The messy problem. Sources disagree. The customer's claim says "storm," the pass log says the antenna tracked cleanly, space weather says the band was quiet, and maintenance was announced three days earlier. Time matters: a March decision should change what the system does in June. Approvers are busy; the controller sometimes says no. Whoever proposes a credit cannot be the one who promotes the rule that allows it. What's real vs simulated. Real: CelesTrak orbital elements + SGP4 for live satellite positions; a handful of Starlink satellites with their own marker; KSAT-scale revenue anchors from the 2025 annual report ( NOK 2.361B / ~$234M , ~2.1M contacts, ~375 antennas); AWS Cedar as the real policy engine; SpacetimeDB Maincloud as the live system of record. Simulated: the claim stream, pass telemetry features, space-weather bands, and maintenance notices that feed each dispute, generated so we can plant known-good and known-bad cases. How we know it works: Break It is our planted-error suite with an answer key. Each attack (inflated amount, duplicate claim, forged station log, fake storm excuse, insider raising their own limit, and more) is run against the old policy and the current policy side by side. Policy version

sections.heading: Did we see something new?
sections.text: A company, problem, or approach we haven't seen made autonomous before. The company / problem. Ground-station SLA credit disputes at operator scale , usage-billed space infrastructure where a few minutes of antenna time become revenue, cash, and next quarter's forecast. Not another SaaS refund bot. The approach. Two-speed autonomy, not one big LLM. A cheap tabular model (System 1) clears confident claims on structured features; an LLM (System 2) only reads sources on the hard cases. Most claims never need the expensive path. devpost_page.title: A.U.R.A. (Awareness Understanding and Ranging Assistant)
devpost_page.tagline: A.U.R.A. is an AI-powered wearable mobility aid combining LiDAR and computer vision to detect nearby obstacles, improve spatial awareness, and empower blind or visually impaired individuals.

sections.text: Inspiration Millions of people with low vision rely on a white cane, which only senses what it physically touches, about a meter ahead and at ground level. It can't say what is in the way, and it can't warn about something approaching. We wanted to build a hands-free assistant that understands the space in front of the wearer and describes it out loud, combining the precise distance sensing of a self-driving car's lidar with the object recognition of modern computer vision. What it does A.U.R.A. is a chest-mounted wearable that watches the path ahead and talks to the wearer. A 2D lidar scans the area in front of the wearer 40 times per second. As an obstacle gets closer, A.U.R.A. beeps faster, from slow beeps at 2 m to a solid tone under 0.75 m. A webcam running a YOLO neural network recognises what is ahead (people, cars, bicycles, chairs, benches and more). A.U.R.A. pairs each object with the lidar's exact distance at that angle and speaks alerts like "person ahead, 2 meters" or "chair on the left, 1 meter". All audio plays through a clip-on JBL Bluetooth speaker, so the wearer's hands stay free. A live dashboard streams over Wi-Fi to any laptop or phone browser, with nothing to install. It shows a radar-style map of the lidar scan, colour-coded alert zones, the camera feed with detection boxes, and labels for every recognised object, so a caregiver or judge can see exactly what the wearer is hearing.
